## Step 4 — Evaluate the model honestly

| Metric | Train (313 rows) | Test (79 rows) |
|---|---|---|
| MAE | 1.3633 | 1.4946 |
| MSE | 3.1929 | 4.1105 |
| RMSE | 1.7869 | 2.0274 |
| R² | 0.6948 | 0.6801 |

Checkpoint — train metrics better than test metrics: **True**

| 5-fold CV | Fold 1 | Fold 2 | Fold 3 | Fold 4 | Fold 5 | Mean | Std |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Test R² | 0.6801 | 0.6546 | 0.6980 | 0.7373 | 0.6583 | 0.6857 | 0.0302 |

**Why the training score alone is not enough.** The training score is measured on the same cars the model used to choose θ0 and θ1, so it only shows how well the line fits data it has already seen; a flexible enough model could memorise the training cars, score perfectly on them and still fail on a new one. Only cars held out from fitting (the test set, or the held-out fold in cross-validation) show how the model does on a car it hasn't seen. Here train R² (0.6948) is above test R² (0.6801), as the checkpoint expects, but only by 0.0147. A straight line has only two parameters and cannot memorise 313 cars, so the size of the gap mostly reflects which 79 cars landed in the test set. This is why the 5-fold result (mean test R² 0.6857, std 0.0302), which averages over five different splits, is the more reliable estimate.


## Step 5 — Multiple linear regression

| Features used (cumulative) | Mean test R² (5-fold) | Std | Change vs previous row |
|---|---|---|---|
| mass_kg | 0.6857 | 0.0302 | — |
| + engine_litres | 0.6913 | 0.0286 | +0.0056 |
| + power_hp | 0.6987 | 0.0288 | +0.0074 |
| + cylinders | 0.6987 | 0.0300 | +0.0000 |
| + year | 0.8022 | 0.0146 | +0.1034 |
| + accel_0_100_s | 0.8002 | 0.0155 | -0.0019 |

**Did test R² improve every time a feature was added?** No. 2 of the 5 additions moved the mean test R² by less than 0.005: `cylinders` (+0.0000), `accel_0_100_s` (-0.0019). Adding `accel_0_100_s` actually lowered it. `cylinders` overlaps with `engine_litres` (r = +0.95), which was already in the model. `accel_0_100_s` overlaps with `power_hp` (r = -0.69), which was already in the model. The biggest gain came from `year` (+0.1034), even though it ranks only #5 of 6 by correlation with the target; it adds information (how new the car is) that the size and power columns do not contain. The model with every numeric feature scores 0.8002, below the best row (0.8022). So throwing every column into the model is not a free improvement: what a feature adds depends on what the model already contains, not on its own correlation with the target. A feature that repeats known information only gives least squares another coefficient to estimate from the same cars, so each addition has to earn its place on held-out data.


## Step 6 — Polynomial regression

| Degree | Train R² (5-fold mean) | Test R² (5-fold mean) | Test R² change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.6924 | 0.6857 | — |
| 2 | 0.7149 | 0.7075 | +0.0218 |
| 3 | 0.7150 | 0.7070 | -0.0005 |
| 4 | 0.7153 | 0.7071 | +0.0001 |
| 5 | 0.7161 | 0.7062 | -0.0009 |

Highest mean test R²: degree **2**

**Where test R² stops improving.** Test R² rises from 0.6857 at degree 1 to 0.7075 at degree 2 and stops improving there: no higher degree beats it by more than 0.005 (degree 3: 0.7070, degree 4: 0.7071, degree 5: 0.7062).

**Why train R² keeps climbing while test R² does not.** Train R² goes from 0.6924 at degree 1 to 0.7161 at degree 5 and never decreases. A higher-degree polynomial contains every lower-degree one (set the extra coefficients to zero), so on the cars it is fitted to it can only match or beat the lower degree. Each extra term is extra freedom to bend the curve toward the particular training cars, including their random scatter. That scatter does not repeat in the held-out fold, so past degree 2 the extra bends buy nothing on test data, or lose a little. Degree 2 already captures the real shape (fuel efficiency falls as `mass_kg` grows, and the curve flattens out at high `mass_kg`), so the higher degrees only fit noise. This relies on standardizing `mass_kg` inside the pipeline first: its raw values span 732–2331, so the degree-5 term would reach about 6.9e+16, which makes plain least squares numerically unstable.


## Step 7 — Conclusion

I would use the multiple linear regression from Step 5 on 5 features: `mass_kg`, `engine_litres`, `power_hp`, `cylinders` and `year`. It has the highest mean 5-fold test R² of every model I fitted, 0.8022, against 0.6857 for simple regression on `mass_kg` and 0.7075 for the best polynomial (degree 2). Its cross-validated RMSE is 1.46 km/L versus 1.84 km/L for `mass_kg` alone, so a typical prediction for a new car is off by about 1.5 km/L. Adding `year` was worth +0.1034 R², while bending the `mass_kg` line into a curve gained only +0.0218. Cars became more efficient over the 1970–1982 model years even at the same `mass_kg`, and no curve in `mass_kg` alone can capture that. I left out `accel_0_100_s`: with every feature the mean test R² is 0.8002, no better than this model, and each extra input is one more thing to measure for a new car. `cylinders` added less than 0.005 R² when it entered the model, so a leaner model without it is worth testing next.

Only 6 of 398 rows (1.51%) were dropped for missing `power_hp`; they come from 5 different model years and 2 regions, and so few rows cannot noticeably move coefficients fitted on the remaining 392 cars. One caution: the model only saw cars from 1970–1982, so its `year` effect should not be extrapolated to modern cars.
